title: Nickel-catalyzed ring-opening difunctionalization of methylenecyclobutanes via strain-release-enabled C-C activation

paper_content.abstract: The efficient construction of molecular complexity from simple building blocks is a significant goal in catalysis, and the controlled ring-opening functionalization of strained carbocycles provides a powerful strategy to achieve it. However, selective catalytic strategies for ring-opening difunctionalization of methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs) remain elusive. Here, we report a nickel-catalyzed method that enables the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization and 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs via selective C–C bond cleavage. This protocol exploits the strain energy and dual reactivity of MCBs to deliver nonadjacent C(sp³)/C(sp²) frameworks in good to excellent yields under mild conditions. A broad substrate scope, scalability to the gram scale, and versatile downstream transformations demonstrate the synthetic utility of this approach. Mechanistic studies, including control, isotope-labeling experiments, and DFT calculations, reveal a distinct cooperative pathway involving strain-driven β-carbon elimination, offering new opportunities for catalyst-controlled activation of MCBs.
paper_content.introduction:
The efficient assembly of molecular complexity from simple building blocks is a significant goal in catalysis,1-3 with profound implications for synthetic chemistry, drug discovery, and materials science. In this context, catalytic multicomponent reactions that form multiple carbon–carbon bonds in a single step under mild conditions are desirable for generating molecular complexity because they enhance atom economy, reduce waste, and streamline synthetic design.4,5 Among these, the difunctionalization of unsaturated hydrocarbons has become a key strategy,6-8 enabling the selective addition of two different functional groups to access a variety of C(sp³)- and C(sp²)-hybridized frameworks commonly found in bioactive molecules and functional materials,9-11 thus making the synthesis of functional molecules easier.

A breakthrough in this field has been the 1,2-difunctionalization of terminal alkenes and alkynes (Fig. 1A),12-15 which is made possible by their readily available nature, and has advanced significantly through transition-metal catalysis (Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Pd, etc.),16-22 photocatalysis,23-25 electrocatalysis,26 and synergistic techniques27. However, these approaches typically produce either two C(sp³)– or two C(sp²)– hybridized carbon centers, thereby limiting access to molecules with differently hybridized carbon groups. The ability to simultaneously build both C(sp³) and C(sp²) centers in one step remains a key challenge with broad implications for molecular design and increasing complexity. In this regard, terminal allenes stand out as especially useful substrates, offering a solution to this challenge due to their orthogonal π-systems and distinct electronic properties (Fig. 1B).28,29 Their regio- and chemoselective difunctionalization enables the concurrent formation of C(sp³)/C(sp²) centers, providing a more straightforward route to densely functionalized, three-dimensional structures that are difficult to access using traditional alkene or alkyne methods. This reactivity has greatly expanded the synthetic toolkit for creating complex, sophisticated molecules. Inspired by recent advances, efforts have shifted toward strain-activated olefin surrogates such as methylenecyclopropanes (MCPs) (Fig. 1C),30-32 which replace the π-bond of alkenes with a highly strained three-membered ring. These MCPs exhibit allene-like reactivity in transition-metal-catalyzed 1,3-difunctionalization, allowing the simultaneous formation of two nonadjacent C(sp³)/C(sp²) frameworks via strain-release pathways,33-36 which have made significant progress over the past years.

Similar to MCPs, methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs) are versatile organic reagents in chemical synthesis, offering a built-in reservoir of strain energy (strain energy of cyclobutane: 26.5 kcal/mol, cyclopropane: 27.5 kcal/mol) and dual reactivity through their C=C π-system and cyclobutane σ-system37-39. This duality enables transformations via C=C bond difunctionalization or strain-driven C–C bond cleavage, thus significantly enriching the chemical space of MCBs. To date, extensive studies on the applications of methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs) have been reported, with approximately 379 publications and 333 patents documented in SciFinder®. Nevertheless, progress has predominantly focused on 1,2-difunctionalization across the C=C bond40-43 and ring-expansion transformations44-47, whereas ring-opening strategies that enable 1,4-difunctionalization of cyclobutanes through selective C–C bond cleavage remain largely underexplored48, thereby limiting their utility in multicomponent reactions for molecular complexity. Given the high ring strain and electronically unbiased nature of the C=C bonds in methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs), achieving regioselective migratory insertion across these alkenes is both a fundamental challenge and a critical prerequisite for efficient ring-opening functionalization. Recently, Koh and Shi developed a state-of-the-art method for the directing-group-free difunctionalization of unactivated alkenes, and mechanistic insights have shown that bulky Ni–NHC complexes enable the selective difunctionalization of unactivated alkenes by promoting branch-selective migratory insertion of arylmetal species across terminal C=C bonds.49-51 Inspired by this advance, we hypothesized that Ni–NHC catalysis could overcome inherent steric and electronic biases in MCBs, and the branch-selective insertion into the exocyclic methylene group of MCBs would induce strain-driven β-carbon elimination, allowing for direct C–C bond cleavage and subsequent 1,4-difunctionalization (Fig. 1D). This process would produce nonadjacent sp2 and one sp3 carbon centers, which are important building blocks for furnishing many value-added molecules.52,53 Herein, we report a Ni–NHC–catalyzed multicomponent strategy that enables efficient 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization and 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs in this paper.
paper_content.results:
Identification of the catalytic conditions. Initially, we systematically optimized the reaction conditions of the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs via strain-release-enabled ring-opening, selecting 1a, 2a, and 3a as the model substrates. As shown in Table 1, the desired ring-opening product 4a was obtained in 76% yield when the reaction was conducted in cyclohexane using Ni(cod)₂ as the catalyst and nitrogen-heterocyclic carbene (NHC) L6 as the ligand. Replacing L6 with other phosphine or nitrogen-based ligands failed to promote the transformation, highlighting the unique property of L6 in this multicomponent cross-coupling reaction. Further modification of the NHC ligand through steric tuning of the aryl substituents did not enhance the reaction efficiency (L5, 36% yield; L7, 34% yield). Likewise, variations of the imidazole backbone aimed at adjusting both electronic and steric properties failed to improve the yield of 4a (L8, 34% yield; L9, 27% yield; L10, 47% yield), indicating that an appropriate balance of steric and electronic effects is crucial for this transformation and reinforcing L6 as the optimal choice. Solvent screening revealed that low-polarity solvents were more suitable for the reaction, with toluene and PhCF₃ yielding comparable yields of 66% and 73%, respectively. Variations in reaction temperature and substrate concentration were also explored, but no further improvements in yield were observed (see Supplementary Information for details). Notably, reducing the catalyst loading to 1 mol% Ni(cod) still afforded the desired product 4a in 56% yield (see Supplementary Information for details).

Substrate scope. With the optimized conditions established, we next evaluated the substrate scope to assess the generality of the approach for the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs (Fig. 2). We began by examining the electrophilic coupling partners (ArOTf) bearing various substituents to explore electronic and steric effects. Para-substituted aryl triflates with alkyl, trifluoromethoxy, fluoro, or methoxy groups produced the desired products in good yields (45–83%, 4a–4i). Similarly, meta-substituted analogues with comparable functionalities were well tolerated, giving products in 64–81% yield (4j–4o). Next, we explored the substrate scope of nucleophiles with a range of alkylmagnesium chlorides, all of which reacted smoothly under standard conditions to give the ring-opening products in 75–84% yield (4p–4w). In contrast, arylmagnesium halides did not produce the desired products; instead, only Kumada-type cross-coupling products54 between the aryl nucleophiles and ArOTf were detected by GC-MS analysis, highlighting the difficulty of achieving selective ring-opening in the presence of aryl nucleophiles. We also investigated the structural diversity of MCB substrates. Substrates bearing quaternary carbon centers were generally well tolerated, giving moderate to good yields (4x–4ah, 40–81%), indicating minimal steric interference. However, those containing tertiary carbon centers gave the corresponding products 4ai and 4aj in lower yields (34% and 37%) despite their high conversions, which can be attributed to the competitive β-hydride elimination to furnish the 1,4-dienes.55 Additionally, the structure of 4ah was confirmed unambiguously by single-crystal X-ray analysis.

To further extend the utility of the method, we investigated the 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs (Fig. 3). Following systematic optimization (see Supplementary Information), the optimal conditions employed ligand L5 and sodium tert-pentoxide in THF, with aryl bromides as the electrophiles and sodium isopropoxide as the hydrogen source. In contrast, the use of aryl triflates, chlorides, or aryl iodides as electrophilic coupling partners resulted in diminished yields compared to the aryl bromides (see Supplementary Information, Table S6). Moreover, GC-MS analysis revealed the formation of 1,2-hydrocarbofunctionalization byproducts under these conditions, indicating that the nature of the anion plays a crucial role in governing the β-C elimination process. Under the optimal conditions, the target product 7a was obtained in 88% yield. A variety of aryl bromides bearing alkyl, ether, amino, trifluoromethyl, halogen, and fused-ring substituents were well tolerated, affording products 7b–7r in 40–85% yield. Notably, heteroaryl bromides could also undergo 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization, delivering 7s–7u in 30–63% yield. Furthermore, a highly conjugated substrate, 1,1,2,2-tetrakis(4-bromophenyl)ethene, could be employed to furnish tetraphenylethylene derivative 7v in 37% yield, potentially enabling access to new fluorescent scaffolds.56,57 Finally, a broad range of MCBs was subjected to 1,4-hydrocarbonation under the optimized conditions. As shown in Fig. 3 (7w–7ag), MCBs with quaternary carbon centers furnished products in up to 95% yield. Remarkably, tertiary-substituted MCBs were also well tolerated, affording 7ah–7am in 64–86% yield.

Applications of the method. To underscore the versatility and practical value of this method, gram-scale reactions and diverse downstream transformations were carried out. As shown in Fig. 4A, both 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization and 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs proceeded efficiently on a gram-scale under standard conditions, delivering the desired products in high yields (7a, 86%; 4a, 59%). The operational simplicity of the protocol was further demonstrated by employing the air-stable Ni(0) precatalyst Ni(4-tBustb) ,58,59 which enabled the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of 1a to furnish 4a in a reduced yield of 52% (Fig. 4B), likely due to the steric bulk of Ni(4-tBustb) . Collectively, these results underscore the scalability and robustness of the method. Importantly, selective hydrogenation and oxidation of the sterically hindered C=C bond were achieved under mild conditions (Fig. 4C), showcasing excellent functional group tolerance and enabling access to structurally diverse alkanes 8 (79% yield) and 9 (51% yield). Moreover, the cobalt/photoredox-catalyzed difunctionalization of 7a delivered ketone 11 in 73% yield (Fig. 4D),60 further demonstrating the synthetic utility of the products. Notably, the bisphenol derivative as an important monomer for polycarbonate resins was synthesized in 42% yield over two steps via difunctionalization of 12 followed by demethylation (Fig. 4E), underscoring the method’s potential for constructing functional materials.

Mechanistic evaluation. Mechanistic insights were elucidated through control experiments, isotope-labeling studies (Fig. 5), and DFT calculations (Fig. 6). Complete reaction blockage without benzylmagnesium chloride (3a) and the absence of Heck-type byproducts when 2a was omitted confirm the crucial roles of both reagents in enabling C–C single-bond cleavage of MCBs (Fig. 5A). 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionation of 1a with sodium deuterated isopropoxide produced the fully deuterated product (>99% D, confirmed by 1H-NMR analysis), clearly indicating the alkoxide as the hydride source.61 Substituting sodium isopropoxide with sodium 1-phenylethan-1-olate produced 7a (38% yield) along with acetophenone (detected by GC–MS analysis), providing further evidence for this hydride transfer pathway (Fig. 5B). Additionally, a significant kinetic isotope effect (KIE = 3) suggests that hydride transfer is likely the rate-determining step. Furthermore, the radical-trapping experiments for the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization using one equivalent of TEMPO or BHT afforded 4a in 62% yield and 66% yield, respectively, thereby excluding the involvement of a radical pathway (Fig. 5C). In addition, Ni(IPr) was evaluated as a catalyst for the dicarbofunctionalization of 1a, delivering 4a in a 43% yield (Fig. 5D), which supports the participation of an active Ni–NHC catalytic species.

To gain deeper insight into the reaction mechanism, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed (see Supplementary Information for computational details). Substrates 1a', 2b and 3a were selected as model systems. The computed free-energy profiles for the formation of products P1 and P2 are summarized in Fig.6, while an alternative pathway leading to P1 is depicted in Fig. S14. Initial coordination of PhOTf to the active Ni0(NHC) species is exergonic, affording intermediate int1 (ΔG = −21.0 kcal/mol), which undergoes irreversible oxidative addition via TS1 to generate the Ni(II) species int2. Subsequent coordination of alkene 1a' to int2 leads to the formation of four-coordinate Ni–MCB complexes int3 and int3', corresponding to the precursors of TS2 and TS2', respectively. Notably, formation of both int3 and int3' is endergonic, indicating that alkene coordination is thermodynamically uphill. Consequently, the free-energy barriers for olefin insertion are referenced to int2. From int2, 1,2-insertion via TS2 is favored over the competing 2,1-insertion pathway (TS2'), and the 1,2-insertion step exhibits the highest activation free energy of the catalytic cycle, identifying it as the rate-determining step.

Following olefin insertion, the resulting alkyl-Ni(II) intermediate int4 represents a key branching point of the reaction manifold. As shown in Fig. 6, int4 preferentially undergoes transmetalation with Grignard reagent 3a to generate alkyl-Ni(II)-benzyl species int5. Subsequent isomerization affords int6, in which the alkyl and benzyl groups adopt a trans relationship. From int6, β-carbon elimination proceeds via TS3, involving C–C σ-bond cleavage accompanied by π-bond formation, to give intermediate int7. Further isomerization leads to int8, which undergoes C–C reductive elimination via TS4 to furnish product P1. Alternatively, int5 can directly undergo reductive elimination through TS3' to form product P2. This direct reductive elimination pathway is kinetically less favorable, with an activation barrier of 17.8 kcal/mol relative to int5, and also thermodynamically disfavored compared to P1 formation, consistent with the experimental observations.

In addition to the pathway shown in Fig.6, Fig. S14 illustrates an alternative pathway, in which β-carbon elimination precedes transmetalation. In this scenario, int4 first undergoes β-C elimination, followed by transmetalation, isomerization, and reductive elimination to ultimately afford product P1. Importantly, the activation barriers associated with the elementary steps following int4 along both pathways are substantially lower than that of the olefin insertion step. Therefore, while the pathway in Fig. 6 is kinetically preferred, the competing pathway shown in Fig. S14 cannot be excluded and may operate in parallel after the rate-determining olefin insertion step.

In summary, we have developed a broad nickel–NHC-catalyzed strategy for the selective ring-opening 1,4-difunctionalization of methylenecyclobutanes, including hydrocarbonation and dicarbonation. This catalyst-controlled approach allows efficient access to molecules with nonadjacent C(sp³) and C(sp²) centers through strain-release pathways under mild conditions. The method’s broad functional group tolerance, scalability, and diverse post-functionalization options demonstrate its practicality for building structurally complex molecules. Detailed mechanistic studies and DFT calculations reveal the potential pathway, expanding the synthetic toolkit for challenging C–C bond cleavage and opening new avenues for designing complex molecular architectures in synthetic chemistry and drug discovery. Moreover, ongoing work in our lab on diverse 1,4-difunctionalization of MCBs will be reported in due course.
paper_content.methods:
General procedure for the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs. In a N -filled glove box, an oven-dried 4 mL vial equipped with a stir bar was charged with Ni(cod) (10 mol%), L6 (10 mol%), and cyclohexane (1.0 mL). Grignard reagent 3 (0.3 mmol, 3.0 equiv.) was slowly added to the system subsequently. The reaction mixture was allowed to stir at room temperature for 0.5 h. Methylenecyclobutene 1 (0.1 mmol 1.0 equiv.) and aryl triflate 2 (0.2 mmol 2.0 equiv.) were then added to the system. The vial was sealed and the reaction mixture was allowed to stir at 40 oC for 24 h. After cooling to ambient temperature, the crude mixture was quenched with aqueous NH Cl. The mixture was diluted with ethyl acetate (5 mL), washed with brine, dried over Na₂SO₄, and purified by flash column chromatography to afford the desired products 4.

General procedure for the 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs. In a N -filled glove box, an oven-dried 4 mL vial equipped with a stir bar was charged with Ni(cod) (10 mol%), L5 (10 mol%), t-AmONa (25 mol%) and THF (1.0 mL). The reaction mixture was allowed to stir at room temperature for 10 minutes. Aryl bromide 5 (0.2 mmol, 2.0 equiv.), cyclobutene 1 (0.1 mmol, 1.0 equiv.), and sodium isopropoxide (0.3 mmol, 3.0 equiv.) were then added to the system. The vial was sealed and the reaction mixture was allowed to stir at 40 0C for 12 h. After cooling to ambient temperature, the crude mixture was quenched with aqueous NH Cl. The mixture was diluted with ethyl acetate (5 mL), washed with brine, dried over Na₂SO₄, and purified by flash column chromatography to afford the desired products 7.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, Wang and co-workers report a novel NHC-Ni-catalyzed, ring-opening multicomponent reaction of
methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs), leveraging ring-strain release to drive either 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization or 1,4-
hydrocarbofunctionalization. The strategy effectively harnesses the strain energy and dual reactivity of MCBs, providing
access to valuable nonadjacent C(sp³)/C(sp²) frameworks with high efficiency and broad substrate scope. The synthetic
utility of this method is demonstrated through a series of downstream transformations. The proposed mechanism, supported
by control experiments and detailed DFT calculations, involves a key strain-driven β-carbon elimination. Based on the
reviewer’s research experience in the chemistry of alkylidenecyclopropanes and alkylidenecyclobutanes, this study
represents a significant contribution to small-ring chemistry and is recommended for publication in Nature Communications
after the following minor issues are addressed:
1. While this paper examines diverse methylenecyclobutanes via NHC-Ni catalysis, extending the study to include
methylenecyclopropanes under the standard conditions would enhance broad readership appeal. Additionally, control
experiments using methylenecyclopentane and methylenecyclohexane are necessary to clarify the critical role of ring strain.
2. Given that benzocyclobutenones serve as valuable building blocks for synthesizing valuable molecules through C–C
activation, it would be worthwhile to examine whether this method is applicable to benzocyclobutenone-derived alkenes
(e.g., 7-methylenebicyclo[4.2.0]octa-1,3,5-triene). Such an exploration could open new chemical space.
3. For the 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization process, although sodium isopropoxide demonstrated high reactivity as a
hydrogen source, evaluating other hydride sources (e.g., silanes and isopropanol) would provide a more comprehensive
understanding of the reaction scope.
4. From an electronic perspective, benzylmagnesium chloride represents a somewhat unique class of Grignard reagents.
The reviewer suggests that the authors explore the reactions of other alkyl Grignard reagents, such as n-butylmagnesium
chloride and cyclohexylmagnesium chloride.
5. Formatting and labeling corrections:
Line 52: According to the literature data (Chem. Rev. 2021, 121, 264−299), “cyclobutene” should be revised to “cyclobutane”
(26.5 kcal/mol).
Fig. 1: “underdevelopment” should be revised to “underdeveloped”.
Line 101: Compound 4i is not a meta-substituted product.
Line 103: “4o-4v” should be revised to “4o-4w”.
Line 108: “4w-4ah” should be revised to “4x-4ah”.
Line 185: “intramolecular” should be removed.
Line 212 and 220: “cyclobutene” should be revised to “methylenecyclobutane”.
6. The crystal structure identifier requires correction in the manuscript.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
The present manuscript reports a nickel-catalyzed selective ring-opening and subsequent functionalization of
methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs) through controlled C–C bond cleavage. This approach enables both 1,4-
dicarbofunctionalization and 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization, by effectively transforming the intrinsic ring strain and dual
reactivity of MCBs into a powerful tool for building nonadjacent C(sp³)–C(sp²) frameworks. The reactions proceed under mild
conditions, delivering the intended products in high yields. The present work is supported by experimental optimization, a
broad substrate scope, scalability studies, and detailed mechanistic insights corroborated by DFT calculations. Overall, the
manuscript may be considered for publication in Nat. Commun. after the authors address the following major concerns.
1. In general, oxidative addition is preferable when a metal centre is electron rich. Between the ligand L6/L7, the L7
containing LNi0 containing species is supposed to be more electron rich however, the optimisation conditions suggest that
L6 provides better yield. The authors should provide suitable justification/theoretical explanation to support their observation.
2. Authors should perform reaction by combining the present NHC-Ni system with other chelating ligands like dppe, dppf,
dcype etc., which together may yield better catalytic system.
3. In the substrate scope table Fig. 2 from 4p to 4aj and in Fig. 3 from 7w to 7am there is a specific choice of p-
methoxyphenyl triflate as coupling partner when there is variation in MCBs. Authors need to justify why there is such
specificity.
4. “The operational simplicity of the protocol was further demonstrated by employing the air-stable Ni(0) precatalyst Ni(4-
tBustb)3, which enabled the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of 1a to furnish 4a in 52% yield (Fig. 4B).” In this context there is a
lack of clarity that why does Ni(4-tBustb)3 provides lesser yield. Is it governed by both steric and electronic factors?
5. The control experiment section looks weak as there is no such clarity about how the Ni-NHC complex is significantly
involved in the catalytic cycle. The authors should provide evidence for the active Ni-NHC catalyst.
6. In the control experiment, no radical quenching experiment has been performed. However, there is a possibility that
present reaction may proceed through radical pathway. Hence, the authors should perform quenching experiments to
exclude a radical pathway.
7. The optimization table shows that NHC ligand (L6) works well for 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs. The manuscript
would benefit from a more detailed discussion of the steric and electronic properties that make L6 is most effective compared
to other ligands.
8. The proposed β-carbon elimination pathway is plausible and well-supported by DFT. However, direct experimental
evidence (such as detection of intermediates or kinetic studies) is limited. The authors should provide additional mechanistic
insights - such as stoichiometric reactions or trapping of Ni-alkyl intermediates to reinforce the proposed sequence.
9. The authors note the suppression of 1,2-difunctionalization and Kumada-type cross-coupling side reactions. However, no
rationale is provided for how the catalyst system selectively promotes 1,4-difunctionalization over other possible coupling
modes. Clarifying the factors (steric, electronic, or strain-release effects) controlling this selectivity would enhance
mechanistic understanding.
10. The author should provide a clear rationale explaining why the L5 ligand is particularly effective for the 1,4-
hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs, whereas the L6 ligand performs better in the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
The authors present a nice study of Ni-catalyzed difunctionalization of methylenecyclobutanes, exploiting the strain energy
and dual reactivity of MCBs to obtain nonadjacent C(sp3)/C(sp2) frameworks. The mechanism is further disclosed by both
experiment and DFT study, preliminarily revealed the reaction mechanism. However, the reaction mechanism needs to be
improved and the computational results were not clearly expressed in pictures, and the discussion was not sufficient. In
addition, the computed energy barrier of 27.3 kcal/mol for the 1,2-insertion step is too high for the reaction at 40 °C.
Therefore, I suggest the authors resubmit it for review after major revision noted below.
1) Despite the fact that for square planar Ni(II) complexes, the singlet state is typically the ground state, the energy
differences of the spin-polarized singlet and triplet states for tri-coordinate Ni complexes are still worth considering.
2) The rate-determine-step (RDS) of calculated mechanism seems to be the insertion step with 27.3 kcal/mol energy barrier
as shown in Fig. 5c in page 10 of the manuscript. Although kinetic isotope effect indicates a RDS participated with the
functionalization of the sp3-C, for different reactants, ArMgCl and iPrONa, the reaction mechanism may differ, leading to
inconsistent RDS. Therefore, the lower activation energy of int8 to TS4 (21.0 kcal/mol) comparing with that of int5' to TS4
(26.3 kcal/mol) in the competing reaction pathway introduced in SI, cannot determine the advantage or disadvantage of the
reaction pathway, since both two energy barriers are available under experimental temperature (313 K) and lower than the
activation energy of int2 to TS2. I suggest that the author reconsider the two reaction pathways, RDS, and possibly
supplement the experiment of the kinetic isotope effect corresponding to ArMgCl.
3) The pre-intermediate of TS2 and TS2', a four-coordinate Ni-MCB complex, should be under discussion instead of
skipping. Although from the experimental results I can easily infer that TS2' does not take advantages, as mentioned in 2), I
believe it is necessary to consider the pre-intermediate to further clarify the details of this step. Similar issues arise during the
transition from int3 to int4, due to the presence of the competing transition state TS2'' and the energetic irreversibility of the
3a coordination process (from int3 to int4 and from int3' to int4'), the transition state of this process needs to be clarified.
4) In my opinion, the pre-intermediate of TS3' should not be int6 but int5. The relative position of two groups in TS3' is more
similar to int5 instead of int6.
5) The distinction between the int5' and int8 cannot be discerned from Figure S13, I suggest adding a 3D structural diagram
for support. Furthermore, the possibility of int5' and int7 undergoing reductive elimination is worth exploring. I am confused
by the necessity of passing through int8 before reductive elimination can occur.
6) I hope to obtain some conjectures or arguments for the following questions related to reactivity: the possible reason of the
influence of substituents on the reactants and ligands; the reason for using L5 with lower yield instead of L6 in the
computation.
7) Regarding the plotting of potential energy profiles, I suggest the following: strive to maintain a higher energy level for the
front part of int2 relative to the rear part to avoid unnecessary misunderstandings; set the endpoint of the reaction pathway to
Ni(0)L and detach the product to construct a complete catalytic cycle.
8) The reaction time should be added to Figs. 2 and 3. The yield of 4a should be indicated in Fig. 2 to facilitate direct
comparison. The structure of 1a should be presented in a consistent manner in Supplementary Sections 5.11 and 5.12.
9)In Fig. 5, the reaction-energy profile presented by the authors contains obvious errors; for example, TS2 is placed at –42.5
kcal mol⁻¹ yet is drawn higher than TS1 at –11.1 kcal mol⁻¹.

recommendation, we have examined additional alkyl Grignard reagents as shown below,
including n-butylmagnesium bromide and cyclohexylmagnesium bromide. Unfortunately,
these reagents were incompatible with our catalytic system, and no desired product was
detected by GC–MS analysis. Further investigations aimed at optimizing the catalytic
system and expanding its generality are currently underway, which we expect will open
new avenues for the divergent transformation of methylenecyclobutanes.
5. Formatting and labeling corrections:

should be revised to “cyclobutane” (26.5 kcal/mol).
Fig. 1: “underdevelopment” should be revised to “underdeveloped”.

Response: We thank the reviewer for these suggestions. We have corrected these

Reviewer #2 (Remarks to the Author):
The present manuscript reports a nickel-catalyzed selective ring-opening and subsequent
functionalization of methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs) through controlled C–C bond cleavage.
This approach enables both 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization and 1,4-
hydrocarbofunctionalization, by effectively transforming the intrinsic ring strain and dual
reactivity of MCBs into a powerful tool for building nonadjacent C(sp³)–C(sp²) frameworks.
The reactions proceed under mild conditions, delivering the intended products in high
yields. The present work is supported by experimental optimization, a broad substrate
scope, scalability studies, and detailed mechanistic insights corroborated by DFT
calculations. Overall, the manuscript may be considered for publication in Nat. Commun.
after the authors address the following major concerns.
Response: We sincerely thank this reviewer for the positive comments on our work, we
really appreciate it.
1. In general, oxidative addition is preferable when a metal centre is electron rich. Between
the ligand L6/L7, the L7 containing LNi0 containing species is supposed to be more
electron rich however, the optimisation conditions suggest that L6 provides better yield.
The authors should provide suitable justification/theoretical explanation to support their
observation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. To further elucidate the
role of steric and electronic effects of NHC ligands in this transformation, we evaluated a
broader set of NHC ligands. As shown below, additional modification of the NHC ligand via
steric tuning of the aryl substituents did not enhance the reaction efficiency (L5, 36% yield;
L7, 34% yield). Similarly, variations of the imidazole backbone designed to modulate both
electronic and steric properties failed to improve the yield of 4a (L8, 34%; L9, 27%; L10,
47%), indicating that an appropriate balance of steric and electronic effects is critical for
this transformation.
2. Authors should perform reaction by combining the present NHC-Ni system with other
chelating ligands like dppe, dppf, dcype etc., which together may yield better catalytic
system.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer's insightful suggestion. In response, we evaluated
a range of ligand combinations for this reaction. As shown below, the addition of 10 mol%
dppe under the standard dicarbofunctionalization conditions did not affect the product yield,
whereas reducing the NHC loading to 5 mol% resulted in a decreased yield of 45%.
Moreover, the introduction of additional phosphine ligands failed to enhance the reaction
efficiency, indicating that the incorporation of other chelating ligands is not beneficial for
this catalytic system. Consistent results were also observed in the
hydrocarbofunctionalization reaction, as shown below.
3. In the substrate scope table Fig. 2 from 4p to 4aj and in Fig. 3 from 7w to 7am there is
a specific choice of p-methoxyphenyl triflate as coupling partner when there is variation in
MCBs. Authors need to justify why there is such specificity.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. To systematically evaluate
the structural tolerance of the reaction conditions toward MCBs, it is necessary to employ
a single, well-defined electrophile in accordance with the principle of controlling variables.
Given their ready availability and good functional-group tolerance, p-methoxyphenyl triflate
and p-methoxyphenyl bromide were therefore selected as the coupling partners for this
investigation.
4. “The operational simplicity of the protocol was further demonstrated by employing the
air-stable Ni(0) precatalyst Ni(4-tBustb)3, which enabled the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization
of 1a to furnish 4a in 52% yield (Fig. 4B).” In this context there is a lack of clarity that why
does Ni(4-tBustb)3 provides lesser yield. Is it governed by both steric and electronic factors?
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. As noted by the reviewer,
the reduced yield can be attributed to a combination of steric and electronic factors, which
is further supported by our ligand-screening studies for this transformation. We have
clarified in the revised manuscript that the pronounced steric bulk of Ni(4-tBustb) may
3
impede the reaction efficiency, thereby leading to the diminished yield.
5. The control experiment section looks weak as there is no such clarity about how the Ni-
NHC complex is significantly involved in the catalytic cycle. The authors should provide
evidence for the active Ni-NHC catalyst.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. Following the
recommendation, we synthesized the Ni(IPr) catalyst according to the reported procedure
2
(J. Org. Chem. 82, 6895 – 6903 (2017)). As shown below, the dicarbofunctionalization
reaction proceeded smoothly to afford the desired product in 43% yield, further confirming
the involvement of an active Ni–NHC catalyst. We have added the result to the manuscript.
6. In the control experiment, no radical quenching experiment has been performed.
However, there is a possibility that present reaction may proceed through radical pathway.
Hence, the authors should perform quenching experiments to exclude a radical pathway.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. The radical-trapping
experiments for the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization using one equivalent of TEMPO or BHT
afforded 7a in 62% yield and 66% yield, respectively, thereby excluding the involvement of
a radical pathway. We have added the results to manuscript.
7. The optimization table shows that NHC ligand (L6) works well for 1,4-
dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs. The manuscript would benefit from a more detailed
discussion of the steric and electronic properties that make L6 is most effective compared
to other ligands.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. To further elucidate the
role of steric and electronic effects of NHC ligands in this transformation, we evaluated a
broader set of NHC ligands. As shown below, additional modification of the NHC ligand via
steric tuning of the aryl substituents did not enhance the reaction efficiency (L5, 36% yield;
L7, 34% yield). Similarly, variations of the imidazole backbone designed to modulate both
electronic and steric properties failed to improve the yield of 4a (L8, 34%; L9, 27%; L10,
47%), indicating that an appropriate balance of steric and electronic effects is critical for
this transformation. We have added the results to the manuscript.
8. The proposed β-carbon elimination pathway is plausible and well-supported by DFT.
However, direct experimental evidence (such as detection of intermediates or kinetic
studies) is limited. The authors should provide additional mechanistic insights - such as
stoichiometric reactions or trapping of Ni-alkyl intermediates to reinforce the proposed
sequence.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. To further probe the
mechanism, we conducted a stoichiometric experiment using one equivalent of Ni(cod)₂
and the ligand, as shown below. After stirring for 12 h, 1 mL of H O was added to the
2
reaction mixture, which was then directly analyzed by GC-MS. The formation of the 1,4-
hydrocarbofunctionalization product was observed, thereby supporting the involvement of
a Ni–alkyl intermediate in the catalytic cycle. These results have been included in the
Supplementary Information.
9. The authors note the suppression of 1,2-difunctionalization and Kumada-type cross-
coupling side reactions. However, no rationale is provided for how the catalyst system
selectively promotes 1,4-difunctionalization over other possible coupling modes.
Clarifying the factors (steric, electronic, or strain-release effects) controlling this selectivity
would enhance mechanistic understanding.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. In prior studies (J. Am.
Chem. Soc. 143, 9498−9506 (2021); Nat. Catal. 6, 1087−1097 (2023)), NHC–Ni-catalyzed
regioselective 1,2-difunctionalization of terminal alkenes was largely governed by steric
effects imposed by the catalyst, and the Kumada-type cross-coupling between aryl triflates
and benzylmagnesium chlorides is not fully suppressed and remains a primary competing
pathway. Notably, in contrast to these precedents, the present reaction predominantly
furnishes the 1,4-difunctionalization product, while 1,2-difunctionalization is significantly
disfavored. We attribute this switch in selectivity to the strain-release associated with β-
carbon elimination of the cyclobutene framework, which drives the reaction along the 1,4-
difunctionalization pathway and is confirmed by the DFT calculations.
10. The author should provide a clear rationale explaining why the L5 ligand is particularly
effective for the 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs, whereas the L6 ligand performs
better in the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful suggestion. The 1,4-difunctionalization
of MCBs proceeds in the presence of multiple competing pathways, including 1,2-
difunctionalization across the C=C bond, direct cross-coupling between the electrophile
and nucleophile, and challenges associated with regioselective migratory insertion.
Therefore, precise control over both the steric environment and the electronic properties
of the Ni center is critical.
From our ligand-screening studies, L5 and L6 display distinct reactivity profiles that we
attribute to their different steric and electronic features. L6 possesses a slightly larger
buried volume and stronger σ-donating character, which we propose facilitates the second
C–C bond-forming step while simultaneously reducing side cross-coupling events, leading
to improved yields of the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization product. In contrast, L5 provides a
comparatively less encumbered coordination environment and a weaker σ-donation profile.
We believe this promotes a more facile β-H elimination step and enables subsequent
protonation, which is beneficial under the hydrofunctionalization conditions. As shown
below, for the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of 1a, ligand L6 outperforms L5, as it
significantly suppresses the formation of side products under these conditions. Conversely,
in the 1,4-hydrofunctionalization of 1a, ligand L5 delivers superior results, owing to its
greater ability to minimize competitive by-product formation.
Taken together, these observations support a ligand-controlled mechanistic divergence,
where subtle differences in steric demand and electron donation modulate the balance
between β-carbon elimination, cross-coupling, and protonation steps. Further
investigations on the detailed catalytic mechanism is our ongoing work, which will be
reported in due course.
Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
The authors present a nice study of Ni-catalyzed difunctionalization of
methylenecyclobutanes, exploiting the strain energy and dual reactivity of MCBs to obtain
nonadjacent C(sp3)/C(sp2) frameworks. The mechanism is further disclosed by both
experiment and DFT study, preliminarily revealed the reaction mechanism. However, the
reaction mechanism needs to be improved and the computational results were not clearly
expressed in pictures, and the discussion was not sufficient. In addition, the computed
energy barrier of 27.3 kcal/mol for the 1,2-insertion step is too high for the reaction at 40 °C.
Therefore, I suggest the authors resubmit it for review after major revision noted below.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for the positive evaluation of our work and for
the constructive and insightful comments. In the revised manuscript, we have updated the
DFT calculations for ligand L6 and revised the manuscript according to your comments.
Regarding the comment that “the computed energy barrier of 27.3 kcal/mol for the 1,2-
insertion step is too high for the reaction at 40 °C”, we agree that the absolute value of a
calculated activation barrier should be interpreted with caution when directly compared to
experimental reaction temperatures. It is important to note that the primary goal of the DFT
study in this work is not to reproduce the experimental kinetics quantitatively, but rather to
provide a qualitative and comparative mechanistic framework that rationalizes the
observed regioselectivity.
We again thank the reviewer for this valuable comment, which has helped us to improve
the clarity of the computational results in the revised manuscript.
1. Despite the fact that for square planar Ni(II) complexes, the singlet state is typically the
ground state, the energy differences of the spin-polarized singlet and triplet states for tri-
coordinate Ni complexes are still worth considering.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In line with this suggestion,
we further evaluated the spin-state energetics of the key tri-coordinate Ni intermediates.
As summarized in Table S18 in the Supplementary Information, the calculated Gibbs free
energy differences between the triplet and singlet states (ΔG ) for intermediates int2,
T–S
and int5′ are 15.3, 15.4, and 16.9 kcal/mol, respectively. These calculation results clearly
indicate that the singlet state is strongly favored over the triplet state for these tri-coordinate
Ni species, supporting the validity of describing the reaction pathway on the singlet
potential energy surface.

2. The rate-determine-step (RDS) of calculated mechanism seems to be the insertion step
with 27.3 kcal/mol energy barrier as shown in Fig. 5c in page 10 of the manuscript. Although
kinetic isotope effect indicates a RDS participated with the functionalization of the sp3-C,
for different reactants, ArMgCl and iPrONa, the reaction mechanism may differ, leading to
inconsistent RDS. Therefore, the lower activation energy of int8 to TS4 (21.0 kcal/mol)
comparing with that of int5' to TS4 (26.3 kcal/mol) in the competing reaction pathway
introduced in SI, cannot determine the advantage or disadvantage of the reaction pathway,
since both two energy barriers are available under experimental temperature (313 K) and
lower than the activation energy of int2 to TS2. I suggest that the author reconsider the two
reaction pathways, RDS, and possibly supplement the experiment of the kinetic isotope
effect corresponding to ArMgCl.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful and careful analysis of the calculated
reaction pathways and the interpretation of the rate-determining step (RDS). We agree that
when multiple reaction pathways are kinetically accessible, caution must be exercised in
correlating individual activation barriers with pathway preference.
In the revised manuscript, we have updated the DFT calculations for ligand L6 and
corresponding discussion (now shown in Figure 6 and Figure S14) to more accurately
reflect the mechanistic features of the system. In the updated energy profiles, the olefin
insertion step from int2 to TS2, with an activation free energy of 27.0 kcal/mol, is identified
as the highest barrier shared by all pathways leading to P1 and P2. This step therefore
constitutes the rate-determining step of the catalytic cycle, independent of the subsequent
sequence of elementary steps.
After formation of int4, the reaction bifurcates into two competing pathways that differ in
the order of transmetalation and β-C elimination. Importantly, all subsequent steps along
both pathways exhibit significantly lower activation barriers than that of the olefin insertion
step. As correctly pointed out by the reviewer, under the experimental conditions, these
post-insertion steps are all kinetically accessible and therefore do not determine the overall
reaction rate or uniquely dictate pathway preference. Accordingly, in the revised manuscript,
we no longer rely on comparisons between individual downstream barriers (e.g., reductive
elimination steps) to claim the dominance of one pathway over the other.
3. The pre-intermediate of TS2 and TS2', a four-coordinate Ni-MCB complex, should be
under discussion instead of skipping. Although from the experimental results I can easily
infer that TS2' does not take advantages, as mentioned in 2), I believe it is necessary to
consider the pre-intermediate to further clarify the details of this step. Similar issues arise
during the transition from int3 to int4, due to the presence of the competing transition state
TS2'' and the energetic irreversibility of the 3a coordination process (from int3 to int4 and
from int3' to int4'), the transition state of this process needs to be clarified.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment.
To further clarify the details of the olefin insertion step, we explicitly examined the pre-
intermediates preceding the 1,2- and 2,1-insertion transition states. As shown in Figure 6,
coordination of substrate 1a′ to the Ni(II) center in int2 leads to the formation of four-
coordinate Ni–MCB complexes int3 and int3′, which serve as the immediate precursors to
TS2 and TS2′, respectively. Notably, the formation of both int3 and int3′ from int2 is
calculated to be endergonic, indicating that coordination of the strained
methylenecyclobutane to the Ni center is thermodynamically uphill. As a result, the
effective activation barriers for both the 1,2- and 2,1-insertion pathways are appropriately
referenced to int2, rather than to the higher-energy pre-intermediates. Consequently,
explicit inclusion of these pre-intermediates does not alter the identification of the olefin
insertion step as the rate-determining step of the catalytic cycle.
Regarding the transmetalation step, we fully agree that the full reaction sequence
including the reactant complex, transition state, and product complex should be
characterized. However, despite extensive efforts, we were unable to locate a well-defined
transition state or a stable reactant complex for the transmetalation between intermediate
int4 and the Grignard reagent 3a at the employed level of theory. For the product side, a
stable product complex could only be optimized in the gas phase. Starting from this gas-
phase optimized structure, we subsequently performed a relaxed potential energy surface
(PES) scan, using the C···Mg distance as the reaction coordinate. In this scan, the C···Mg
distance was gradually shortened (from right to left in Figure S13). The resulting energy
profile is shown in Figure S13, which reveals a smooth and barrierless energy descent
without a discernible maximum. Notably, the optimized structures indicate a significant
coordination rearrangement upon association of 3a with int4. Specifically, coordination of
the Grignard reagent to the Ni center induces dissociation of the triflate ligand from Ni,
followed by preferential coordination of OTf⁻ to the Mg center.
Figure S13
4. In my opinion, the pre-intermediate of TS3' should not be int6 but int5. The relative
position of two groups in TS3' is more similar to int5 instead of int6.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment. In the revised calculations,
we carefully reanalyzed the structural relationship between TS3′ and the preceding
intermediates by IRC calculations. By comparing key geometric parameters and the
relative orientations of the alkyl and benzyl fragments, the analysis clearly indicates that
TS3′ evolves directly from int5, rather than int6, as its geometry more closely resembles
that of int5. On this basis, we have reassigned the pre-intermediate of TS3′ to int5, and
the corresponding labeling and mechanistic discussion have been consistently corrected
in Figure 6 and in the revised manuscript.
5. The distinction between the int5' and int8 cannot be discerned from Figure S13, I suggest
adding a 3D structural diagram for support. Furthermore, the possibility of int5' and int7

passing through int8 before reductive elimination can occur.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. In the revised
Supplementary Information, we have provided the optimized structures of intermediates
int5' and int8 (please refer to Figure S15). Intermediate int5' and int8 differ primarily in
the conformation of the alkyl fragment bound to Ni, arising from single-bond rotation along
the Ni–alkyl chain. Importantly, the calculated results indicate that productive C–C
reductive elimination occurs exclusively from int8, with TS4 unambiguously connected to
this intermediate. Attempts to locate a direct reductive elimination transition state from int7
were unsuccessful, indicating that int7 must first undergo isomerization to int8 to achieve
the proper geometry for C–C bond formation. For int5′, this intermediate can undergo
direct C–C reductive elimination via TS4′ (Figure S14), this pathway is kinetically less
favorable due to its higher activation barrier compared to that of TS4.
6. I hope to obtain some conjectures or arguments for the following questions related to
reactivity: the possible reason of the influence of substituents on the reactants and ligands;
the reason for using L5 with lower yield instead of L6 in the computation.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. To ensure consistency with
the experimentally optimal conditions and to avoid ambiguity arising from ligand effects,
we have recalculated the entire reaction mechanism using ligand L6. All computational
data, energy profiles, and mechanistic discussions in the revised manuscript are now
exclusively based on the L6-ligated Ni catalyst. The corresponding figures, tables, and
mechanistic analyses have been revised accordingly in the manuscript and Supplementary
Information.
7. Regarding the plotting of potential energy profiles, I suggest the following: strive to
maintain a higher energy level for the front part of int2 relative to the rear part to avoid
unnecessary misunderstandings; set the endpoint of the reaction pathway to Ni(0)L and
detach the product to construct a complete catalytic cycle.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s constructive suggestions on the presentation of
the potential energy profiles. In the revised manuscript, Figure 6 has been modified
following the reviewer’s suggestions. Specifically, the relative energy level of the front
segment of int2 has been adjusted to avoid potential confusion in reading the energy
profile. In addition, the reaction pathway is now extended to terminate at the regenerated
Ni(0)L species with explicit dissociation of the organic product, thus depicting a complete
and closed catalytic cycle. These revisions improve the clarity and consistency of the
energy diagram and more accurately reflect the catalytic nature of the process.
8. The reaction time should be added to Figs. 2 and 3. The yield of 4a should be indicated
in Fig. 2 to facilitate direct comparison. The structure of 1a should be presented in a
consistent manner in Supplementary Sections 5.11 and 5.12.
Response: We thank the reviewer for this suggestion. We have corrected these mistakes
in the manuscript and supplementary information.
9. In Fig. 5, the reaction-energy profile presented by the authors contains obvious errors;
for example, TS2 is placed at –42.5 kcal mol⁻¹ yet is drawn higher than TS1 at –11.1 kcal
mol⁻¹.
Response: In the revised manuscript, Figure 6 has been modified in accordance with the
reviewer’s suggestions to provide a clearer depiction of the energy profile.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

The efficient construction of molecular complexity from simple building blocks is a significant goal in catalysis, and the controlled ring-opening functionalization of strained carbocycles provides a powerful strategy to achieve it. However, selective catalytic strategies for ring-opening difunctionalization of methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs) remain elusive. Here, we report a nickel-catalyzed method that enables the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization and 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs via selective C–C bond cleavage. This protocol exploits the strain energy and dual reactivity of MCBs to deliver nonadjacent C(sp³)/C(sp²) frameworks in good to excellent yields under mild conditions. A broad substrate scope, scalability to the gram scale, and versatile downstream transformations demonstrate the synthetic utility of this approach. Mechanistic studies, including control, isotope-labeling experiments, and DFT calculations, reveal a distinct cooperative pathway involving strain-driven β-carbon elimination, offering new opportunities for catalyst-controlled activation of MCBs.

---

## Introduction

The efficient assembly of molecular complexity from simple building blocks is a significant goal in catalysis,1-3 with profound implications for synthetic chemistry, drug discovery, and materials science. In this context, catalytic multicomponent reactions that form multiple carbon–carbon bonds in a single step under mild conditions are desirable for generating molecular complexity because they enhance atom economy, reduce waste, and streamline synthetic design.4,5 Among these, the difunctionalization of unsaturated hydrocarbons has become a key strategy,6-8 enabling the selective addition of two different functional groups to access a variety of C(sp³)- and C(sp²)-hybridized frameworks commonly found in bioactive molecules and functional materials,9-11 thus making the synthesis of functional molecules easier.

A breakthrough in this field has been the 1,2-difunctionalization of terminal alkenes and alkynes (Fig. 1A),12-15 which is made possible by their readily available nature, and has advanced significantly through transition-metal catalysis (Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Pd, etc.),16-22 photocatalysis,23-25 electrocatalysis,26 and synergistic techniques27. However, these approaches typically produce either two C(sp³)– or two C(sp²)– hybridized carbon centers, thereby limiting access to molecules with differently hybridized carbon groups. The ability to simultaneously build both C(sp³) and C(sp²) centers in one step remains a key challenge with broad implications for molecular design and increasing complexity. In this regard, terminal allenes stand out as especially useful substrates, offering a solution to this challenge due to their orthogonal π-systems and distinct electronic properties (Fig. 1B).28,29 Their regio- and chemoselective difunctionalization enables the concurrent formation of C(sp³)/C(sp²) centers, providing a more straightforward route to densely functionalized, three-dimensional structures that are difficult to access using traditional alkene or alkyne methods. This reactivity has greatly expanded the synthetic toolkit for creating complex, sophisticated molecules. Inspired by recent advances, efforts have shifted toward strain-activated olefin surrogates such as methylenecyclopropanes (MCPs) (Fig. 1C),30-32 which replace the π-bond of alkenes with a highly strained three-membered ring. These MCPs exhibit allene-like reactivity in transition-metal-catalyzed 1,3-difunctionalization, allowing the simultaneous formation of two nonadjacent C(sp³)/C(sp²) frameworks via strain-release pathways,33-36 which have made significant progress over the past years.

Similar to MCPs, methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs) are versatile organic reagents in chemical synthesis, offering a built-in reservoir of strain energy (strain energy of cyclobutane: 26.5 kcal/mol, cyclopropane: 27.5 kcal/mol) and dual reactivity through their C=C π-system and cyclobutane σ-system37-39. This duality enables transformations via C=C bond difunctionalization or strain-driven C–C bond cleavage, thus significantly enriching the chemical space of MCBs. To date, extensive studies on the applications of methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs) have been reported, with approximately 379 publications and 333 patents documented in SciFinder®. Nevertheless, progress has predominantly focused on 1,2-difunctionalization across the C=C bond40-43 and ring-expansion transformations44-47, whereas ring-opening strategies that enable 1,4-difunctionalization of cyclobutanes through selective C–C bond cleavage remain largely underexplored48, thereby limiting their utility in multicomponent reactions for molecular complexity. Given the high ring strain and electronically unbiased nature of the C=C bonds in methylenecyclobutanes (MCBs), achieving regioselective migratory insertion across these alkenes is both a fundamental challenge and a critical prerequisite for efficient ring-opening functionalization. Recently, Koh and Shi developed a state-of-the-art method for the directing-group-free difunctionalization of unactivated alkenes, and mechanistic insights have shown that bulky Ni–NHC complexes enable the selective difunctionalization of unactivated alkenes by promoting branch-selective migratory insertion of arylmetal species across terminal C=C bonds.49-51 Inspired by this advance, we hypothesized that Ni–NHC catalysis could overcome inherent steric and electronic biases in MCBs, and the branch-selective insertion into the exocyclic methylene group of MCBs would induce strain-driven β-carbon elimination, allowing for direct C–C bond cleavage and subsequent 1,4-difunctionalization (Fig. 1D). This process would produce nonadjacent sp2 and one sp3 carbon centers, which are important building blocks for furnishing many value-added molecules.52,53 Herein, we report a Ni–NHC–catalyzed multicomponent strategy that enables efficient 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization and 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs in this paper.

---

## Results

Identification of the catalytic conditions. Initially, we systematically optimized the reaction conditions of the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs via strain-release-enabled ring-opening, selecting 1a, 2a, and 3a as the model substrates. As shown in Table 1, the desired ring-opening product 4a was obtained in 76% yield when the reaction was conducted in cyclohexane using Ni(cod)₂ as the catalyst and nitrogen-heterocyclic carbene (NHC) L6 as the ligand. Replacing L6 with other phosphine or nitrogen-based ligands failed to promote the transformation, highlighting the unique property of L6 in this multicomponent cross-coupling reaction. Further modification of the NHC ligand through steric tuning of the aryl substituents did not enhance the reaction efficiency (L5, 36% yield; L7, 34% yield). Likewise, variations of the imidazole backbone aimed at adjusting both electronic and steric properties failed to improve the yield of 4a (L8, 34% yield; L9, 27% yield; L10, 47% yield), indicating that an appropriate balance of steric and electronic effects is crucial for this transformation and reinforcing L6 as the optimal choice. Solvent screening revealed that low-polarity solvents were more suitable for the reaction, with toluene and PhCF₃ yielding comparable yields of 66% and 73%, respectively. Variations in reaction temperature and substrate concentration were also explored, but no further improvements in yield were observed (see Supplementary Information for details). Notably, reducing the catalyst loading to 1 mol% Ni(cod) still afforded the desired product 4a in 56% yield (see Supplementary Information for details).

Substrate scope. With the optimized conditions established, we next evaluated the substrate scope to assess the generality of the approach for the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs (Fig. 2). We began by examining the electrophilic coupling partners (ArOTf) bearing various substituents to explore electronic and steric effects. Para-substituted aryl triflates with alkyl, trifluoromethoxy, fluoro, or methoxy groups produced the desired products in good yields (45–83%, 4a–4i). Similarly, meta-substituted analogues with comparable functionalities were well tolerated, giving products in 64–81% yield (4j–4o). Next, we explored the substrate scope of nucleophiles with a range of alkylmagnesium chlorides, all of which reacted smoothly under standard conditions to give the ring-opening products in 75–84% yield (4p–4w). In contrast, arylmagnesium halides did not produce the desired products; instead, only Kumada-type cross-coupling products54 between the aryl nucleophiles and ArOTf were detected by GC-MS analysis, highlighting the difficulty of achieving selective ring-opening in the presence of aryl nucleophiles. We also investigated the structural diversity of MCB substrates. Substrates bearing quaternary carbon centers were generally well tolerated, giving moderate to good yields (4x–4ah, 40–81%), indicating minimal steric interference. However, those containing tertiary carbon centers gave the corresponding products 4ai and 4aj in lower yields (34% and 37%) despite their high conversions, which can be attributed to the competitive β-hydride elimination to furnish the 1,4-dienes.55 Additionally, the structure of 4ah was confirmed unambiguously by single-crystal X-ray analysis.

To further extend the utility of the method, we investigated the 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs (Fig. 3). Following systematic optimization (see Supplementary Information), the optimal conditions employed ligand L5 and sodium tert-pentoxide in THF, with aryl bromides as the electrophiles and sodium isopropoxide as the hydrogen source. In contrast, the use of aryl triflates, chlorides, or aryl iodides as electrophilic coupling partners resulted in diminished yields compared to the aryl bromides (see Supplementary Information, Table S6). Moreover, GC-MS analysis revealed the formation of 1,2-hydrocarbofunctionalization byproducts under these conditions, indicating that the nature of the anion plays a crucial role in governing the β-C elimination process. Under the optimal conditions, the target product 7a was obtained in 88% yield. A variety of aryl bromides bearing alkyl, ether, amino, trifluoromethyl, halogen, and fused-ring substituents were well tolerated, affording products 7b–7r in 40–85% yield. Notably, heteroaryl bromides could also undergo 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization, delivering 7s–7u in 30–63% yield. Furthermore, a highly conjugated substrate, 1,1,2,2-tetrakis(4-bromophenyl)ethene, could be employed to furnish tetraphenylethylene derivative 7v in 37% yield, potentially enabling access to new fluorescent scaffolds.56,57 Finally, a broad range of MCBs was subjected to 1,4-hydrocarbonation under the optimized conditions. As shown in Fig. 3 (7w–7ag), MCBs with quaternary carbon centers furnished products in up to 95% yield. Remarkably, tertiary-substituted MCBs were also well tolerated, affording 7ah–7am in 64–86% yield.

Applications of the method. To underscore the versatility and practical value of this method, gram-scale reactions and diverse downstream transformations were carried out. As shown in Fig. 4A, both 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization and 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs proceeded efficiently on a gram-scale under standard conditions, delivering the desired products in high yields (7a, 86%; 4a, 59%). The operational simplicity of the protocol was further demonstrated by employing the air-stable Ni(0) precatalyst Ni(4-tBustb) ,58,59 which enabled the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of 1a to furnish 4a in a reduced yield of 52% (Fig. 4B), likely due to the steric bulk of Ni(4-tBustb) . Collectively, these results underscore the scalability and robustness of the method. Importantly, selective hydrogenation and oxidation of the sterically hindered C=C bond were achieved under mild conditions (Fig. 4C), showcasing excellent functional group tolerance and enabling access to structurally diverse alkanes 8 (79% yield) and 9 (51% yield). Moreover, the cobalt/photoredox-catalyzed difunctionalization of 7a delivered ketone 11 in 73% yield (Fig. 4D),60 further demonstrating the synthetic utility of the products. Notably, the bisphenol derivative as an important monomer for polycarbonate resins was synthesized in 42% yield over two steps via difunctionalization of 12 followed by demethylation (Fig. 4E), underscoring the method’s potential for constructing functional materials.

Mechanistic evaluation. Mechanistic insights were elucidated through control experiments, isotope-labeling studies (Fig. 5), and DFT calculations (Fig. 6). Complete reaction blockage without benzylmagnesium chloride (3a) and the absence of Heck-type byproducts when 2a was omitted confirm the crucial roles of both reagents in enabling C–C single-bond cleavage of MCBs (Fig. 5A). 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionation of 1a with sodium deuterated isopropoxide produced the fully deuterated product (>99% D, confirmed by 1H-NMR analysis), clearly indicating the alkoxide as the hydride source.61 Substituting sodium isopropoxide with sodium 1-phenylethan-1-olate produced 7a (38% yield) along with acetophenone (detected by GC–MS analysis), providing further evidence for this hydride transfer pathway (Fig. 5B). Additionally, a significant kinetic isotope effect (KIE = 3) suggests that hydride transfer is likely the rate-determining step. Furthermore, the radical-trapping experiments for the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization using one equivalent of TEMPO or BHT afforded 4a in 62% yield and 66% yield, respectively, thereby excluding the involvement of a radical pathway (Fig. 5C). In addition, Ni(IPr) was evaluated as a catalyst for the dicarbofunctionalization of 1a, delivering 4a in a 43% yield (Fig. 5D), which supports the participation of an active Ni–NHC catalytic species.

To gain deeper insight into the reaction mechanism, density functional theory (DFT) calculations were performed (see Supplementary Information for computational details). Substrates 1a', 2b and 3a were selected as model systems. The computed free-energy profiles for the formation of products P1 and P2 are summarized in Fig.6, while an alternative pathway leading to P1 is depicted in Fig. S14. Initial coordination of PhOTf to the active Ni0(NHC) species is exergonic, affording intermediate int1 (ΔG = −21.0 kcal/mol), which undergoes irreversible oxidative addition via TS1 to generate the Ni(II) species int2. Subsequent coordination of alkene 1a' to int2 leads to the formation of four-coordinate Ni–MCB complexes int3 and int3', corresponding to the precursors of TS2 and TS2', respectively. Notably, formation of both int3 and int3' is endergonic, indicating that alkene coordination is thermodynamically uphill. Consequently, the free-energy barriers for olefin insertion are referenced to int2. From int2, 1,2-insertion via TS2 is favored over the competing 2,1-insertion pathway (TS2'), and the 1,2-insertion step exhibits the highest activation free energy of the catalytic cycle, identifying it as the rate-determining step.

Following olefin insertion, the resulting alkyl-Ni(II) intermediate int4 represents a key branching point of the reaction manifold. As shown in Fig. 6, int4 preferentially undergoes transmetalation with Grignard reagent 3a to generate alkyl-Ni(II)-benzyl species int5. Subsequent isomerization affords int6, in which the alkyl and benzyl groups adopt a trans relationship. From int6, β-carbon elimination proceeds via TS3, involving C–C σ-bond cleavage accompanied by π-bond formation, to give intermediate int7. Further isomerization leads to int8, which undergoes C–C reductive elimination via TS4 to furnish product P1. Alternatively, int5 can directly undergo reductive elimination through TS3' to form product P2. This direct reductive elimination pathway is kinetically less favorable, with an activation barrier of 17.8 kcal/mol relative to int5, and also thermodynamically disfavored compared to P1 formation, consistent with the experimental observations.

In addition to the pathway shown in Fig.6, Fig. S14 illustrates an alternative pathway, in which β-carbon elimination precedes transmetalation. In this scenario, int4 first undergoes β-C elimination, followed by transmetalation, isomerization, and reductive elimination to ultimately afford product P1. Importantly, the activation barriers associated with the elementary steps following int4 along both pathways are substantially lower than that of the olefin insertion step. Therefore, while the pathway in Fig. 6 is kinetically preferred, the competing pathway shown in Fig. S14 cannot be excluded and may operate in parallel after the rate-determining olefin insertion step.

In summary, we have developed a broad nickel–NHC-catalyzed strategy for the selective ring-opening 1,4-difunctionalization of methylenecyclobutanes, including hydrocarbonation and dicarbonation. This catalyst-controlled approach allows efficient access to molecules with nonadjacent C(sp³) and C(sp²) centers through strain-release pathways under mild conditions. The method’s broad functional group tolerance, scalability, and diverse post-functionalization options demonstrate its practicality for building structurally complex molecules. Detailed mechanistic studies and DFT calculations reveal the potential pathway, expanding the synthetic toolkit for challenging C–C bond cleavage and opening new avenues for designing complex molecular architectures in synthetic chemistry and drug discovery. Moreover, ongoing work in our lab on diverse 1,4-difunctionalization of MCBs will be reported in due course.

---

## Methods

General procedure for the 1,4-dicarbofunctionalization of MCBs. In a N -filled glove box, an oven-dried 4 mL vial equipped with a stir bar was charged with Ni(cod) (10 mol%), L6 (10 mol%), and cyclohexane (1.0 mL). Grignard reagent 3 (0.3 mmol, 3.0 equiv.) was slowly added to the system subsequently. The reaction mixture was allowed to stir at room temperature for 0.5 h. Methylenecyclobutene 1 (0.1 mmol 1.0 equiv.) and aryl triflate 2 (0.2 mmol 2.0 equiv.) were then added to the system. The vial was sealed and the reaction mixture was allowed to stir at 40 oC for 24 h. After cooling to ambient temperature, the crude mixture was quenched with aqueous NH Cl. The mixture was diluted with ethyl acetate (5 mL), washed with brine, dried over Na₂SO₄, and purified by flash column chromatography to afford the desired products 4.

General procedure for the 1,4-hydrocarbofunctionalization of MCBs. In a N -filled glove box, an oven-dried 4 mL vial equipped with a stir bar was charged with Ni(cod) (10 mol%), L5 (10 mol%), t-AmONa (25 mol%) and THF (1.0 mL). The reaction mixture was allowed to stir at room temperature for 10 minutes. Aryl bromide 5 (0.2 mmol, 2.0 equiv.), cyclobutene 1 (0.1 mmol, 1.0 equiv.), and sodium isopropoxide (0.3 mmol, 3.0 equiv.) were then added to the system. The vial was sealed and the reaction mixture was allowed to stir at 40 0C for 12 h. After cooling to ambient temperature, the crude mixture was quenched with aqueous NH Cl. The mixture was diluted with ethyl acetate (5 mL), washed with brine, dried over Na₂SO₄, and purified by flash column chromatography to afford the desired products 7.
